title: 20 Questions With Krewella: After Leaving Music for Two Years, the Duo Returns With a New Album
summary: The Yousaf sisters release, Peak, their first album since 2022, on Sept. 4. "I tried not loving music, and I'm back," says Yasmine. "Jahan knows exactly what I mean."
contentText:
While in the studio working on new music, Krewella — sisters Jahan and Yasmine Yousaf — thought a lot about what it means to peak.

They were aware, of course, that the word can be derogatory when used to reference someone whose biggest accomplishments are behind them. But they found so many other layers to the concept, considering the futility of just continually chasing peak moments, what it means to be truly accomplished — and how, for them, real success comes from life’s lowest moments, as well as its highest ones.

While the sisters have been making inventive, thoughtful, banging dance music since they arrived on the scene in 2012, they could only have made their new album now. Called Peak , the project is a summation of the sisters’ states of mind, with its 12 songs considering love, spirituality, aging, grief, joy and other subjects, taken on with wisdom and reverence and set to productions dually delicate and throttling.

Peak is Krewella’s first album since 2022, with the duo completely stepping away from music for two years before returning to the studio, realizing that expressing themselves through the format is less a career path, and more a fundamental part of who they are.

Here, the sisters talk about making the album, what they learned from the Nervo sisters and what it really means to peak.

1. Where are you in the world right now, and what’s the setting like?

Jahan: We are in Los Angeles both at our separate places, but we live pretty close by, so we get to walk to each other’s places for studio time. For me, the setting is without air conditioning, so I have a lot of fans blowing. I’m burning some incense right now, so the vibes are here.

Yasmine: I’m a four-minute walk from Jahan. If we couldn’t live together, we had to live in the same neighborhood. I’m in my living room, because it has the best natural light — but the real reason I’m here is because our dog is on the couch next to me, and I wanted to be near her, and she won’t come in the studio where I usually work.

2. What is the first album or piece of music you bought for yourself, and what was the medium?

Jahan: Kill Hannah’s Wake Up the Sleepers . It’s a band from Mat Devine from Chicago. He stumbled upon us on MySpace way back in the day when we were dropping demos there and invited me to sing backup vocals on two songs on his band’s album. It was my first time sharing my voice in that way and recording in a professional studio, so it felt like a really big deal for me. I bought the album because of that, and I remember going to Best Buy to purchase it.

Yasmine: We didn’t buy music. We had a local library that had an insane arsenal of CDs, so we would go and surf through thousands of CDs. You were only allowed to take home eight at a time. This is before I knew anything about anyone and I was just going purely based off of what was on the CD cover, but the first one I took home was The Cranberries’ Wake Up and Smell the Coffee . The album had all those giant red spheres on it. I was like, “This looks cool,” and it ended up being one of the soundtracks of my childhood.

3. What did your parents do for a living when you were kids, and what do they think of what you guys do for work now?

Yasmine: Our mom was a self-employed graphic designer until she retired three years ago. She dropped out of college, went into the workforce and worked her way up to the point that she was her own boss. She did catalogs and circulars for the furniture industry for decades. She was just a one-woman powerhouse. She was always working, always on call, ready to make changes, sometimes working 12-to-14-hour days. We’re really proud that she retired, because she was obsessed with working. Our dad ended up as a real estate agent here in Los Angeles, but he also retired last year.

Jahan: As far as what they think of what we’re doing, they’re both very supportive. In the beginning, I think they were skeptical and concerned. But the older I get, the more I’m understanding of that, because you want your child to be taken care of. You want them to have health insurance. You want them to have a sense of financial stability, and the path of an artist doesn’t always guarantee that.

So they were concerned, but also supported us however they could. Our mom loaned us money for our first microphone, and once we started touring, our father was front row in the VIP at our shows. Considering the cultural background he has, being an immigrant from Pakistan, he’s had to break past a lot of his own cultural conditioning to fully embrace us being tattooed women at nightclubs around a bunch of people that have been drinking. We’re very grateful that he’s trusted us and that we have that intimate relationship with him, where we can confide in him and update him on what we’re experiencing in our personal lives and career.

4. What is the first non-gear thing you bought for yourselves when you started making money as artists?

Jahan: When we signed a record deal with Columbia, which made me feel a sense of legitimacy and being taken care of, the first thought was like, “I can now go to Whole Foods and just rack up the bill with all kinds of healthy food items and not have to worry about it.” That was literally the first thought that came into my mind, investing in good-quality food.

Yasmine: My first big purchase was my first pair of eyeglasses that I had put off my whole life, because I just didn’t want to spend the money. I finally bought myself glasses so I could see. It’s crazy to put that off.

5. If you had to recommend one album for someone looking to get into electronic music, what album would you give them?

Yasmine: Just because I saw them at Just Like Heaven last weekend, LCD Soundsystem ‘s Sound of Silver is legendary, and if you want to understand why dance music is what it is today, that’s one of the essentials. It’s punk and dance and so many amalgamations of what was happening in music at one time. Even if you don’t love it, just listen to it to understand historically what was happening in dance music.

Jahan: It’s Bloc Party ‘s Silent Alarm . I just listened to it all the way through for the first time in a few years, and I was reminded of what an incredible, exquisite, excellent album it is from top to bottom. There are no filler songs, and there’s so much energy with the drum work and guitar riffs.

6. What’s the last song you listened to?

Yasmine: This morning I was driving us from the gym to go get coffee, and I put on Rival Console’s Persona , which is one of the most interesting dance records I’ve heard in a long time.

Jahan: “Ecstasy” by ATB, but the Morten Granau remix. I could never get tired of “Ecstacy” by ATB, and the remix does the original song justice, but also creates a fresh way to receive it. That song literally is ecstasy. It creates this sparkle and shimmer in your mood. Whenever I’m in a funk, I turn it on and it immediately helps me have a more hopeful perspective on things.

7. Your new album is called Peak . What’s the meaning of the title?

Yasmine: How much time do we have? [ Laughs. ] When Jahan and I were conceptualizing this album, we had hours of conversations around what it means to us. I still don’t feel like we have our elevator pitch, because it’s so layered. It started as a thought that I had back in 2023, before we had started working on this record. That word kept coming up for me, because there’s a lot of negative and positive feelings around it. We’ve heard people talk about us or other artists like we’ve peaked, or [the word references] high moments in someone’s life.

Everything we talk about is very “as above, so below,” so…
